case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Fourth Circuit improperly granted federal habeas relief by departing from AEDPA’s constraints and the party-presentation/exhaustion rules—effectively relying on unexhausted or unpresented Sixth Amendment impartial-jury theories rather than applying AEDPA deference to the claim actually litigated (ineffective assistance tied to a Remmer-type juror-taint issue).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2254 (AEDPA—exhaustion, deference/“clearly established Federal law” limits), and the Sixth Amendment right to an impartial jury (implicated through juror-extraneous-information/Remmer framework and Strickland ineffective assistance).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Maryland officials) argue the Fourth Circuit granted relief in a way that is ‘untenable’ under binding Supreme Court precedent by (1) bypassing AEDPA’s exhaustion and deferential-review requirements, (2) invoking a vague ‘special circumstances’ exception to reach issues not properly raised/exhausted, (3) violating the principle of party presentation by constructing a new Sixth Amendment impartial-jury/structural-error theory not argued by Sweeney, and (4) failing to apply the correct AEDPA standard to the only exhausted claim (ineffective assistance for not seeking/obtaining a proper Remmer hearing about a juror’s unauthorized scene visit/extraneous exposure).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Sweeney) argues summary reversal is unwarranted because the Fourth Circuit’s decision was not a clear, indisputable departure from settled law and turned on case-specific matters; the party-presentation objection is overstated because Sweeney’s filings raised the core taint/impartial-jury and related duty-to-investigate points such that the issues ‘permeated’ the proceedings; and, in any event, alleged errors are factbound and do not present a clean, broad legal question justifying extraordinary intervention (especially via summary reversal).
key_precedents: Castro v. United States, 540 U.S. 375 (2003) (Scalia, J., concurring)
Major League Baseball Players Ass’n v. Garvey, 532 U.S. 504 (2001)
Eaton v. City of Tulsa, 415 U.S. 697 (1974)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that juror-impartiality facts are intertwined with Strickland prejudice when counsel allegedly failed to pursue a Remmer-type inquiry—does not justify the Fourth Circuit’s approach because AEDPA still requires claim- and adjudication-specific review of the Strickland theory the state court actually decided. As Justice Kavanaugh underscores with Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano, we cannot supply “clearly established” law at a high level of generality to mandate a particular remedial path or to treat unresolved juror influence as a structural-error shortcut around § 2254(d) deference. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Sineneng-Smith also reinforces the institutional cost of appellate reframing that effectively changes the merits theory and risks bypassing exhaustion and deference. The legitimacy-preserving disposition is to reverse or at least vacate and remand for a faithful § 2254(d) application to the exhausted Strickland/Remmer-investigation claim, without announcing broader habeas rules about juror taint.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that juror impartiality is intertwined with Strickland’s deficiency and prejudice inquiries, so the Fourth Circuit might be read as simply unpacking the exhausted IAC claim. But AEDPA’s text channels federal review to the specific claim “adjudicated on the merits” in state court and measures unreasonableness against clearly established holdings for that claim; as Justice Kavanaugh notes (citing Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano), we may not define the governing law at a high level of generality or convert Strickland into a freestanding structural-error/impartial-jury rule. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are also right that Sineneng-Smith’s party-presentation principle matters here because the Fourth Circuit’s reframing effectively supplies a new merits theory as the basis for habeas relief, bypassing § 2254(d) deference and § 2254(b) exhaustion. Even taking the taint allegations seriously, the proper course is to confine relief analysis to the exhausted Strickland/Remmer-investigation theory under AEDPA’s demanding standard rather than treating juror-taint as an independent shortcut to relief.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point—that assessing Strickland prejudice for failure to seek a Remmer-type inquiry necessarily involves asking what juror-taint facts would have been found—does not justify the Fourth Circuit’s move under AEDPA. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, § 2254(d) is claim- and adjudication-specific: the federal court must evaluate whether the state court unreasonably applied clearly established Strickland to the IAC theory actually decided, not effectively award relief on a freestanding impartial-jury/structural-error premise. Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop reinforce that “clearly established” law cannot be stated at a high level of generality to manufacture a Remmer-hearing entitlement on habeas, and Sineneng-Smith underscores the institutional costs of appellate reframing that bypasses deference and exhaustion. The practical consequence of accepting Sotomayor’s approach would be to invite end-runs around AEDPA in juror-taint cases, undermining finality and federalism without a clear statutory or precedential warrant.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side point remains that juror-taint evidence is functionally inseparable from Strickland prejudice when counsel allegedly failed to pursue a Remmer-type inquiry, so the Fourth Circuit could be seen as simply completing the IAC analysis. But Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s institutional critique persuades me that, under AEDPA, the federal court cannot sidestep § 2254(d) by treating unresolved juror influence as if it were a freestanding Sixth Amendment/structural-error entitlement rather than asking whether the state court unreasonably applied Strickland on the specific claim it adjudicated. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano materially tightens the “clearly established law” frame: Strickland’s general investigation duty cannot be leveraged at a high level of generality to constitutionalize a particular Remmer-hearing step on habeas. Sineneng-Smith, as Roberts underscores, confirms the party-presentation/federalism costs of appellate reframing here, so the proper disposition is to vacate/reverse for faithful, claim-specific AEDPA review rather than affirm on an effectively recharacterized theory.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that you cannot do Strickland prejudice for a failure-to-seek-Remmer inquiry without asking what an inquiry would have revealed about juror impartiality, so the Fourth Circuit could be framed as staying within the exhausted IAC claim. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh are right that AEDPA’s § 2254(d) review is claim- and adjudication-specific: the federal court must measure the state court’s Strickland merits decision against clearly established holdings applicable to that Strickland theory, not use Remmer or “structural” language to sidestep deference. Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop, as Kavanaugh notes, sharpen the problem with defining “clearly established law” at too high a level of generality; they make it difficult to treat Remmer as a clearly established, outcome-determinative requirement within Strickland under AEDPA. And Roberts’s Sineneng-Smith point matters pragmatically and institutionally: allowing appellate reframing here would invite habeas courts to relitigate convictions on court-generated theories, undermining Congress’s workable federalism design in AEDPA.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor presses the best counterpoint: that juror-impartiality facts are intertwined with Strickland deficiency and prejudice, so the Fourth Circuit might be understood as merely completing the exhausted IAC claim. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, AEDPA is claim- and adjudication-specific, and § 2254(d) does not permit a federal court to grant relief by functionally converting an IAC/Remmer-investigation theory into a freestanding Sixth Amendment structural-error/impartial-jury claim or by stating “clearly established” law at too high a level of generality. Justice Kavanaugh’s citations to Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop reinforce that constraint: we must identify a clearly established holding that the state court unreasonably applied on the particular Strickland theory actually adjudicated, not derive a broad investigative mandate from Remmer. Sineneng-Smith, invoked by Roberts, also underscores the institutional harm in appellate reframing that bypasses exhaustion and deference, so I remain for petitioner.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point remains that Strickland prejudice for failing to seek a Remmer-type inquiry necessarily asks what such an inquiry would have shown about juror taint, so the Fourth Circuit could be read as staying within the exhausted IAC claim. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, AEDPA’s § 2254(d) review is tethered to the specific claim and the state court’s actual merits adjudication, and we cannot bypass deference by recasting the analysis as a freestanding impartial-jury/structural-error theory. Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop confirm that “clearly established” law cannot be framed at a high level of generality to dictate a particular investigative step or hearing on habeas, and Sineneng-Smith reinforces the institutional/party-presentation problem with the court of appeals’ reframing. The appropriate course is to vacate or reverse for faithful application of § 2254(d) to the Strickland/Remmer-investigation theory as adjudicated by the state court, without structural-error shortcuts.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that juror-impartiality evidence may be inseparable from Strickland prejudice when the alleged deficiency is counsel’s failure to seek a Remmer-type inquiry, so the Fourth Circuit could be read as simply completing the IAC analysis. But as the Chief Justice notes (invoking Sineneng-Smith), the party-presentation and exhaustion framework matters institutionally: a federal court cannot “complete” Strickland by recasting the theory into a freestanding impartial-jury/structural-error claim that the state courts did not adjudicate, thereby evading § 2254(d) deference. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano reinforces the textual, claim-specific constraint: “clearly established Federal law” must be a holding applicable to the particular claim and theory adjudicated, and Remmer cannot be used at too high a level of generality to dictate habeas relief. On this record, the proper course is to confine review to the exhausted Strickland claim as adjudicated and ask only whether that decision was unreasonable under AEDPA’s demanding standard, not to award relief via reframing.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest counterargument—pressed most forcefully by Justice Sotomayor—is that juror-impartiality facts are inseparable from Strickland’s deficiency and prejudice analysis when counsel fails to pursue a Remmer-type inquiry, so the Fourth Circuit was simply completing the IAC inquiry. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively show that AEDPA still requires claim- and adjudication-specific review: the federal court must ask whether the state court unreasonably applied clearly established Strickland to the IAC theory actually decided, not award relief by effectively treating unresolved juror taint as a freestanding Sixth Amendment/structural-error shortcut. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano reinforces that we cannot state “clearly established” law at a high level of generality to mandate a particular investigative or hearing procedure on habeas, and Sineneng-Smith underscores the institutional costs of appellate reframing that bypasses deference and exhaustion. Under a pragmatic, procedure-focused lens, the legitimacy- and administrability-preserving path is to reverse or vacate-and-remand for faithful § 2254(d) application to the exhausted Strickland claim, rather than bless a reframing that would invite routine end-runs around AEDPA in juror-taint cases.

John Roberts.reasoning: AEDPA tightly cabins federal habeas review to claims properly exhausted in state court and adjudicated on the merits, and it requires deference unless the state decision is contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b)(1), (d); see also Marshall v. Rodgers, 569 U.S. 58, 62–64 (2013). To the extent the Fourth Circuit granted relief by reframing the case into a freestanding Sixth Amendment impartial-jury/structural-error theory not fairly presented and then bypassing AEDPA’s constraints, that departs from the adversarial party-presentation principle (United States v. Sineneng-Smith, 590 U.S. 371, 375 (2020)) and risks undermining institutional legitimacy through an unnecessarily broad, nonminimalist approach. The proper course is to confine review to the exhausted Strickland claim tied to the alleged Remmer-type juror taint and apply § 2254(d) deference to the state court’s adjudication rather than create and decide new theories on habeas.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: AEDPA’s text squarely limits federal habeas relief to claims adjudicated on the merits in state court, and permits relief only if the state decision was contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law. See 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1). The Fourth Circuit erred by effectively granting relief on an unexhausted or newly constructed Sixth Amendment impartial-jury/structural-error theory, contrary to the party-presentation principle recognized in Sineneng-Smith, and by failing to apply AEDPA deference to the only properly litigated claim (Strickland ineffective assistance tied to a Remmer-type juror-taint issue). This Court has repeatedly admonished that lower courts may not use habeas to announce or extend rules beyond our holdings—especially under § 2254(d)—as in Shoop v. Cassano and Marshall v. Rodgers, and summary reversal is warranted when that constraint is disregarded.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: AEDPA strictly limits federal habeas relief to claims that were properly exhausted and adjudicated on the merits in state court, and it permits relief only if the state decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d); § 2254(b)(3). The Fourth Circuit’s approach—crediting an expanded Sixth Amendment impartial-jury/structural-error theory not fairly presented and then not applying AEDPA deference to the Strickland/Remmer-tethered ineffective-assistance claim actually litigated—conflicts with this Court’s repeated admonitions that federal courts may not grant habeas relief by recasting claims or relying on legal theories not anchored in clearly established law governing the specific claim. See Shoop v. Cassano and Marshall v. Rodgers. And construing the case to decide on grounds the parties did not present contravenes the party-presentation principle reaffirmed in United States v. Sineneng-Smith, with serious practical consequences for finality and state criminal judgments.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: AEDPA’s constraints in 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d) and exhaustion principles are real, but they do not require federal courts to ignore an inadequately investigated juror-taint record where the petitioner’s litigated Strickland claim (Strickland v. Washington) squarely turns on whether counsel failed to pursue a meaningful inquiry into extraneous influence implicating the Sixth Amendment. The Fourth Circuit’s reasoning, while arguably infelicitously framed, can be understood as addressing the same core exhausted claim—ineffective assistance tied to a Remmer-type impartial-jury problem—rather than manufacturing a wholly new, unexhausted structural-error theory, making summary reversal inappropriate given the case-specific posture and the practical risk of leaving a potentially tainted verdict unremedied. Sineneng-Smith’s party-presentation principle cautions against appellate “takeover,” but it does not bar a court from faithfully resolving the claim’s necessary components where juror impartiality concerns permeate the proceedings and the remedy sought is tethered to the Strickland/Remmer inquiry. Given the liberty stakes and the centrality of an impartial jury, I would not use AEDPA formalism to foreclose relief where the state adjudication unreasonably failed to grapple with the juror-taint investigation that Strickland requires.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: AEDPA limits federal habeas to claims that were properly exhausted and then adjudicated on the merits in state court, and it further requires deference unless the state court’s decision was contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law. See 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b)(1), (d); Marshall v. Rodgers, 569 U.S. 58 (2013). On this record, the Fourth Circuit appears to have granted relief by reshaping the case into an unpresented Sixth Amendment impartial-jury/structural-error theory rather than applying § 2254(d) to the only litigated claim—Strickland ineffective assistance tied to the requested Remmer-type inquiry—contrary to the party-presentation limits emphasized in Sineneng-Smith. Because a court of appeals cannot evade AEDPA’s constraints by deciding a materially different, unexhausted theory on its own initiative, summary correction is warranted.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: AEDPA’s text requires federal courts to deny habeas relief unless the state-court adjudication of the petitioner’s exhausted claim was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law, see 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d), and it also enforces exhaustion as a prerequisite to federal merits relief, § 2254(b). A court of appeals cannot evade those limits by reframing an ineffective-assistance/Remmer investigation claim into a freestanding Sixth Amendment impartial-jury or structural-error theory that was not properly presented and exhausted; doing so both conflicts with AEDPA’s allocation of authority between state and federal courts and violates the party-presentation principle reaffirmed in Sineneng-Smith. This Court has repeatedly cautioned that § 2254(d) is not satisfied by relying on broad generalities or non–clearly-established extensions of precedent, see Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano, and the Fourth Circuit’s approach appears to do just that rather than applying Strickland through AEDPA deference to the claim actually litigated. The proper course is to confine review to the exhausted Strickland claim and apply AEDPA’s deferential standard, not to craft a new Sixth Amendment theory to grant relief.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: AEDPA requires federal habeas courts to adjudicate the claim actually exhausted and decided on the merits in state court, applying deference unless the state-court decision was contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b), (d); see also Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano (warning against defining “clearly established” law at a high level of generality). The Fourth Circuit’s approach—as described—appears to have departed from that framework by effectively reframing the case into an unexhausted Sixth Amendment impartial-jury/structural-error theory rather than applying AEDPA deference to the litigated Strickland/Remmer-type ineffective-assistance claim, and that kind of judicial issue-construction is in tension with the party-presentation principle emphasized in United States v. Sineneng-Smith. Even if courts may sometimes consider certain procedural issues sua sponte (Wood v. Milyard), that limited discretion does not justify bypassing AEDPA’s claim-specific exhaustion and deference rules to grant relief on a theory the state courts were not given a fair opportunity to resolve.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: AEDPA’s text bars federal habeas relief unless the specific claim was adjudicated on the merits in state court and the state decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1). The Fourth Circuit appears to have granted relief by recasting the case into a freestanding Sixth Amendment impartial-jury/Remmer-type theory rather than applying § 2254(d) deference to the exhausted claim actually litigated—Strickland ineffective assistance premised on counsel’s handling of alleged juror taint—contrary to this Court’s repeated insistence that habeas courts may not award relief on unpresented or unadjudicated theories without identifying clearly established law for the claim at issue. See Shoop v. Cassano, 142 S. Ct. 2051 (2022); Marshall v. Rodgers, 569 U.S. 58 (2013). That approach also sits uneasily with the party-presentation principle emphasized in United States v. Sineneng-Smith, 590 U.S. 371 (2020), reinforcing that the court should have confined itself to the claim presented and the limits Congress imposed in AEDPA.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: AEDPA tightly cabins federal habeas review: a federal court may not grant relief unless the state court’s adjudication of the claim presented was contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law, and the exhaustion requirement limits review to claims fairly presented to the state courts. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b), (d). By effectively reframing Sweeney’s Strickland/Remmer ineffective-assistance claim into a freestanding Sixth Amendment impartial-jury/structural-error theory that was not properly presented and then using that reframing to justify relief, the Fourth Circuit risked departing from both AEDPA’s deference and the party-presentation norm this Court enforced in Sineneng-Smith. Even accepting the seriousness of juror-taint allegations under Remmer, the proper course on habeas is to evaluate the exhausted ineffective-assistance claim under AEDPA’s deferential lens rather than build and decide a different constitutional theory in the first instance.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Fourth Circuit improperly granted federal habeas relief by departing from AEDPA’s exhaustion/deference rules and the party-presentation principle—recharacterizing or reaching unpresented Sixth Amendment/juror-bias theories—rather than deciding only the exhausted ineffective-assistance claim under the correct standards.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2254 (AEDPA) (including exhaustion and deferential review) and the Sixth Amendment right to an impartial jury/fair trial (as implicated by alleged juror exposure to extraneous information and Remmer-type procedures).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Maryland (Terence Clark, Director, et al.) argues the Fourth Circuit’s decision is untenable because it (1) effectively reviewed the state-court judgment de novo instead of through AEDPA’s deferential lens, (2) relied on a judge-made 'special circumstances' path to bypass AEDPA exhaustion limits (invoking Frisbie/Granberry), and (3) violated the party-presentation principle by granting relief based on a 'confluence' of constitutional errors and an impartial-jury theory that Sweeney allegedly never raised or exhausted; Maryland also contends Remmer is not clearly established Supreme Court law for a juror’s crime-scene visit, so relief cannot be premised on extending Remmer via circuit precedent.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Sweeney argues summary reversal/certiorari is unwarranted because the issues the Fourth Circuit addressed were not invented by the court but were raised (even if not 'cleanly articulated') throughout his filings and the underlying proceedings; any mistake would be factbound and not implicate broader legal rules, and in any event the case is a poor vehicle for extraordinary intervention since the Fourth Circuit purported to apply Supreme Court precedent to a trial record showing serious juror-taint concerns and failures by both counsel and the trial court to determine the extent of taint before waiver/continuation decisions.
key_precedents: Castro v. United States, 540 U.S. 375 (2003) (Scalia, J., concurring)
Major League Baseball Players Ass’n v. Garvey, 532 U.S. 504 (2001)
Eaton v. City of Tulsa, 415 U.S. 697 (1974)
United States v. Gary, 954 F.3d 194 (4th Cir. 2020)
1988 Tr. for Allen Children v. Banner Life Ins. Co., 28 F.4th 513 (4th Cir. 2022)
Beaudett v. City of Hampton, 775 F.2d 1274 (4th Cir. 1985)
United States v. Bassler, 651 F.2d 600 (8th Cir. 1981)
United States v. Hillard, 701 F.2d 1052 (2d Cir. 1983)
United States v. Perkins, 748 F.2d 1519 (11th Cir. 1984)
Mayhue v. St. Francis Hosp. of Wichita, Inc., 969 F.2d 919 (10th Cir. 1992)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that juror taint strikes at the heart of an impartial jury and creates a powerful equitable pull for federal intervention, but AEDPA does not permit relief on an appellate court’s newly constructed Sixth Amendment/Remmer theory when the only fairly presented claim was Strickland. Justice Alito’s reliance on Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano reinforces that we cannot treat extensions of Remmer—or circuit-law elaborations—as “clearly established” law under § 2254(d)(1), which undercuts the Fourth Circuit’s demanded procedures. Justice Gorsuch’s Sineneng-Smith party-presentation concern is institutionally weighty here: discretion to overlook exhaustion (as in Granberry/Wood) is not discretion to recast the claim and then grant relief on it. The narrow, legitimacy-protecting disposition is to reverse or vacate and remand with instructions to confine review to the exhausted Strickland claim under AEDPA deference, leaving any broader juror-bias theory to state courts in the first instance.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that juror taint is so structurally serious that a federal court may look past exhaustion or reshape the theory to ensure an impartial jury—fails under AEDPA’s text, which contains no freewheeling “structural error” exception to § 2254(b)’s exhaustion rule or § 2254(d)’s limits on granting relief. Chief Justice Roberts is right that the Fourth Circuit’s move departed from party presentation and effectively manufactured a new Remmer-style Sixth Amendment claim rather than adjudicating the exhausted Strickland claim with Richter deference. Justice Alito’s invocation of Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano confirms that circuit-level elaborations of Remmer cannot supply “clearly established Federal law,” so the Fourth Circuit’s demanded procedures rest on an impermissible extension. Even accepting Justice Sotomayor’s fairness concern, the original public meaning of AEDPA requires federal courts to enforce Congress’s constraints, leaving any broader juror-bias theory to be presented to state courts first.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—structural corrosiveness of juror taint—cannot supply an AEDPA “escape hatch” that lets a federal court bypass exhaustion and then award relief on a court-invented Remmer-like Sixth Amendment theory. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Fourth Circuit’s “confluence” reframing clashes with party-presentation limits (Sineneng-Smith) and with § 2254(b)’s exhaustion requirement, and it risks de novo review that § 2254(d) forbids. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano is decisive on the merits: Remmer is not clearly established law for this distinct fact pattern, so extending it (or relying on circuit gloss) cannot justify habeas relief under § 2254(d)(1). The appropriate disposition is reversal (or vacatur/remand) to confine the case to the exhausted Strickland claim under AEDPA’s deferential framework.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—rooted in basic fairness—is that juror taint can be so corrosive that federal courts should intervene even if the precise Sixth Amendment theory was not cleanly exhausted. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, AEDPA’s exhaustion requirement and § 2254(d) deference are structural constraints, not optional equities, and the Fourth Circuit’s “confluence”/Remmer-like reframing effectively created a new claim the state courts were never asked to decide. Justice Alito’s reliance on Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano reinforces that we cannot treat extensions of Remmer (or circuit gloss) as “clearly established” law to justify habeas relief. Even under my pragmatic concern for real-world harms, the legally sustainable remedy is to confine federal review to the exhausted Strickland claim under AEDPA, leaving any broader juror-bias theory to be presented to and addressed by state courts first.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument is that juror-taint allegations are so structural that a federal court may reach an impartial-jury/Remmer theory notwithstanding imperfect exhaustion, but AEDPA’s text provides no such structural-fairness carveout: § 2254(b) requires fair presentation, and § 2254(d) cabins merits relief to unreasonable applications of this Court’s holdings. Chief Justice Roberts’s point is decisive on method and administration: whatever limited discretion Granberry/Wood recognize, it is a discretion that typically enables efficient denial—not the affirmative creation of a new, unexhausted theory to grant relief, especially in tension with party-presentation norms (Sineneng-Smith/Greenlaw). Justice Alito and Justice Thomas further reinforce that the Fourth Circuit’s Remmer expansion cannot supply “clearly established” law under Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano, so the court’s “confluence” approach risks de novo review by another name. The workable, coherent habeas path is vacatur/remand to evaluate the exhausted Strickland claim under AEDPA deference, leaving any distinct juror-bias claim to be exhausted in state court first.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—juror taint is so fundamental that federal courts should reach it despite imperfect exhaustion—cannot overcome AEDPA’s text, which supplies no freestanding “structural error” exception to § 2254(b) or § 2254(d). Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuade me that the Fourth Circuit did not merely apply Strickland but effectively recast the case into a distinct Sixth Amendment/Remmer-style juror-bias claim, violating party-presentation principles (as in Sineneng-Smith and Wood v. Milyard) and sidestepping exhaustion and deference. Justice Alito and Justice Thomas further reinforce that, under Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano, habeas relief cannot rest on extending Remmer (or relying on circuit elaborations) beyond this Court’s clearly established holdings. Even granting the equitable impulse, Granberry/Frisbie-type discretion does not authorize an appellate court to manufacture a new merits theory and award relief on it, so reversal or at least vacatur/remand to the exhausted Strickland claim remains the legally faithful course.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—juror taint as a structural fairness concern—does not authorize a federal court to grant habeas relief on a theory the prisoner did not fairly present to the state courts, and AEDPA contains no such equitable escape hatch. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on exhaustion, party-presentation limits, and § 2254(d) deference is decisive: the Fourth Circuit’s “confluence” rationale effectively reframed an exhausted Strickland claim into an unexhausted Remmer-style impartial-jury claim, the kind of judicial redesign we cautioned against in Sineneng-Smith and policed in Wood v. Milyard. Justice Alito’s reliance on Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano further confirms that circuit elaborations of Remmer cannot supply “clearly established” law under § 2254(d)(1), so even serious juror-taint allegations cannot justify extending our holdings to reach relief. Institutionally, the appropriate course is reversal or at least vacatur/remand to confine the federal courts to the exhausted Strickland claim under AEDPA’s deferential framework, leaving any broader juror-bias theory to be addressed by state courts first.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that juror taint is uniquely corrosive and might, on direct review, trigger something like Remmer’s presumption and hearing requirement; but AEDPA asks a different question—whether the state court unreasonably applied this Court’s clearly established holdings—and Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano foreclose treating lower-court extensions of Remmer as “clearly established.” Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on exhaustion and party presentation is decisive for me: the Fourth Circuit’s “confluence” approach effectively recharacterized an exhausted Strickland claim into an unexhausted Sixth Amendment juror-bias theory, in tension with § 2254(b) and Sineneng-Smith’s limits on court-driven reframing. Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch are also right that any discretion to overlook exhaustion (Granberry/Wood) is not a license to construct a new theory to grant relief, especially where doing so risks de novo review inconsistent with § 2254(d). Nothing in Wood v. Milyard undermines that conclusion; if anything, it underscores the caution collateral-review courts should exercise before injecting and deciding issues the parties did not litigate.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that juror-taint allegations go to the heart of the Sixth Amendment and, as a matter of practical trial fairness, can warrant searching scrutiny; but AEDPA requires that scrutiny to proceed through the claim actually exhausted and adjudicated in state court, here Strickland. Justice Kagan’s party-presentation framing is most persuasive to me institutionally: as she notes (echoing Sineneng-Smith and Wood v. Milyard), the Fourth Circuit’s pivot to a court-constructed Remmer-like impartial-jury theory and “confluence” rationale effectively rewrote the case and then used that rewrite to evade § 2254(b) and (d). Justice Alito’s emphasis on Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano further confirms that even compelling fairness concerns cannot justify extending Remmer or relying on circuit gloss as “clearly established” law under § 2254(d)(1). On a progressive-pragmatist view, predictable and evenhanded habeas administration is itself a fairness value, and the proper course is vacatur/remand to apply AEDPA deference to the exhausted Strickland claim, leaving any broader juror-bias theory to the state courts first.

John Roberts.reasoning: AEDPA requires federal courts to confine habeas relief to properly exhausted claims and to apply deferential merits review under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d), not to pivot to unexhausted Sixth Amendment juror-bias theories or reframe the case beyond what the petitioner fairly presented to the state courts. The Fourth Circuit’s apparent reliance on sua sponte “special circumstances” reasoning (Frisbie/Granberry) to bypass exhaustion, and its granting of relief on a court-constructed “confluence” of errors, raises serious party-presentation concerns under Sineneng-Smith and the limits on courts raising forfeited defenses recognized in Wood v. Milyard. On the merits, granting relief based on extending Remmer-type procedures to a different factual setting risks violating AEDPA’s “clearly established Federal law” constraint as emphasized in Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano. Given the institutional and federalism interests embedded in AEDPA, the appropriate course is reversal or at least a remand directing application of the correct exhaustion/deference framework to the exhausted Strickland claim alone.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: AEDPA’s text strictly cabins federal habeas relief: a writ may issue only if the state court’s adjudication was contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law, or rested on an unreasonable factual determination. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d); Harrington v. Richter. The Fourth Circuit erred by departing from party presentation and the exhausted Strickland posture to award relief on a recharacterized Sixth Amendment juror-bias/Remmer-type theory, effectively diluting AEDPA’s exhaustion/deference regime and venturing beyond "clearly established" law as this Court has repeatedly forbidden. See United States v. Sineneng-Smith; Marshall v. Rodgers; Shoop v. Cassano. Because Remmer cannot be extended via circuit precedent to create clearly established law for § 2254(d)(1) purposes, relief predicated on that expansion cannot stand.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: AEDPA requires federal courts to respect both exhaustion and the deferential standard of review in 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d), and we have repeatedly admonished lower courts not to grant habeas relief by extending precedent beyond “clearly established Federal law.” See Marshall v. Rodgers, 569 U.S. 58 (2013); Shoop v. Cassano, 142 S. Ct. 2051 (2022). The Fourth Circuit’s reliance on an unexhausted or recharacterized impartial-jury/juror-bias theory, and its apparent use of a “confluence” rationale untethered to the properly exhausted ineffective-assistance claim, conflicts with the party-presentation principle and the restraint emphasized in Wood v. Milyard, 566 U.S. 463, 473 (2012), and Sineneng-Smith, 590 U.S. 371 (2020). Even if habeas courts have limited discretion to consider certain forfeited defenses (Granberry v. Greer, 481 U.S. 129 (1987)), that does not justify bypassing AEDPA’s constraints to reach or manufacture new constitutional theories to grant relief. Nor is Remmer v. United States, 347 U.S. 227 (1954), clearly established as requiring the procedures the Fourth Circuit effectively demanded for a juror’s independent crime-scene visit, so relief on that basis amounts to an impermissible expansion under § 2254(d)(1).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: AEDPA requires federal courts to confine habeas relief to claims properly exhausted in state court and to apply deferential review to state-court adjudications, not to recast the case into new Sixth Amendment juror-bias theories on their own initiative. The party-presentation principle likewise limits an appellate court from injecting and deciding unpresented theories, and Sineneng-Smith condemns a court’s drastic departure from the issues the parties framed. Even crediting serious concerns about juror taint, § 2254(d) and this Court’s warnings against extending precedent beyond “clearly established” law (e.g., Marshall v. Rodgers; Shoop v. Cassano) counsel against affirming relief premised on an expanded Remmer-type rule not clearly established for these facts. The proper course is to vacate and remand for consideration of the exhausted ineffective-assistance claim under the correct AEDPA and Strickland standards, rather than affirm relief on a court-constructed “confluence” theory.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: AEDPA requires federal courts to adjudicate only exhausted claims and to apply deferential review to state-court merits determinations. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b), (d). If the only properly exhausted claim is ineffective assistance, the court of appeals cannot effectively grant relief on a different, unexhausted Sixth Amendment juror-bias/Remmer-style theory by reframing the case or aggregating “confluence” errors, because that both bypasses exhaustion and risks de novo review forbidden by § 2254(d) (see also Marshall v. Rodgers; Shoop v. Cassano). And under the party-presentation principle, an appellate court’s drastic recharacterization of the issues—especially to reach a theory the parties did not squarely present—runs into Sineneng-Smith and Greenlaw, absent a clear, explained basis for departing from those norms on collateral review.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: AEDPA’s text, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b)–(d), requires federal courts to confine relief to claims properly exhausted in state court and to apply deferential review to state-court adjudications; a court of appeals may not evade those limits by recasting an exhausted ineffective-assistance claim into a distinct, unexhausted Sixth Amendment juror-bias theory or by inventing a judge-made “special circumstances” workaround. Our adversarial system also demands adherence to party presentation, and when a court “depart[s] so drastically from the principle of party presentation as to constitute an abuse of discretion,” reversal is warranted. United States v. Sineneng-Smith, 590 U.S. 371, 375 (2020); see also Wood v. Milyard, 566 U.S. 463 (2012) (cautioning against courts’ raising of forfeited issues). Finally, even if juror-taint concerns are serious, habeas relief cannot rest on extending Supreme Court precedent beyond “clearly established” law, Marshall v. Rodgers, 569 U.S. 58, 64 (2013), and Remmer does not clearly establish the rule the Fourth Circuit effectively applied here.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a federal court may grant habeas relief only on an exhausted claim and only if the state-court adjudication was contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b), (d); and this Court has repeatedly cautioned against using circuit precedent or extensions of our cases to supply “clearly established” law (Marshall v. Rodgers; Shoop v. Cassano). The Fourth Circuit’s reframing toward an unexhausted impartial-jury/Remmer-type theory and its apparent reliance on a judge-made “special circumstances” bypass risks the kind of departure from party presentation we rejected in Sineneng-Smith and the improper sua sponte alteration of litigated issues we limited in Wood v. Milyard. Given the need for institutional regularity and workable habeas rules, I would vote to reverse/summary vacate and require the court to confine itself to the exhausted ineffective-assistance claim under AEDPA deference.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: AEDPA’s text requires federal courts to respect both exhaustion and the limited, deferential review Congress prescribed in 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b)–(d), and we have repeatedly cautioned that habeas relief cannot rest on de novo reweighing or on expanding “clearly established Federal law” beyond this Court’s holdings. To the extent the Fourth Circuit granted relief by recasting the case into an unexhausted Sixth Amendment juror-bias/Remmer-type claim or by assembling a “confluence” of errors not squarely presented, that approach conflicts with the party-presentation principle reaffirmed in United States v. Sineneng-Smith and with AEDPA limits on courts supplying new theories. Moreover, even if juror-taint concerns are serious, § 2254(d)(1) permits relief only when the state court unreasonably applied this Court’s clearly established precedent, and decisions like Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano forbid using circuit law or extensions of Remmer to satisfy that standard. Because the proper course is to decide the exhausted ineffective-assistance claim under Strickland through AEDPA’s deferential lens, the Fourth Circuit’s departure warrants reversal.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: AEDPA requires federal courts to respect both exhaustion and deferential review of claims “adjudicated on the merits” in state court, see 28 U.S.C. § 2254(b), (d), and we have repeatedly warned that habeas relief cannot rest on de novo reweighing or on extending Supreme Court precedent beyond what is “clearly established,” see Marshall v. Rodgers and Shoop v. Cassano. The Fourth Circuit’s approach—granting relief based on a “confluence” of Sixth Amendment/juror-taint theories that were not cleanly presented or exhausted—raises serious party-presentation and fairness concerns, because appellate courts ordinarily should not recast a case around issues the parties did not litigate, especially on collateral review, see United States v. Sineneng-Smith and Wood v. Milyard. Even accepting that juror exposure allegations are troubling, the proper course under AEDPA is to decide the exhausted ineffective-assistance claim under Strickland and § 2254(d), not to bypass exhaustion/deference through a judge-made “special circumstances” route. A remand for application of the correct AEDPA framework would better protect procedural regularity while still allowing serious constitutional claims to be addressed through the channels Congress prescribed.
